what_it_does: A 5G receiver is the front-end of a smartphone's modem that picks up wireless signals from cell towers. This receiver must handle a 200-megahertz-wide channel of data, which introduces a major challenge: powerful interference signals from nearby channels can overpower the desired signal, a problem called 'blocker tolerance.' This paper describes a receiver that uses aggressive analog filtering — specifically, a fifth-order filter with a steep roll-off (the electrical response gets stronger and stronger at rejecting nearby frequencies). The design uses a mixer-first topology, which is an architecture that immediately converts the incoming radio signal to baseband (a lower frequency easier to work with), combining the filtering and conversion in a clever way. The result achieves 19 dBm of adjacent-channel input intercept point (IIP3) — a measure of how much interference the receiver can withstand — while maintaining low noise and acceptable power consumption.
